plimsoll trainer · 01 / foundations

Concepts

A load line is painted on the outside of a hull, where anyone can read it. plimsoll paints the isolation tier the same way: a value on every response, a floor a caller asserts before anything runs, and a startup check that has to earn the mark before the daemon will serve. Seven ideas, one page, starting with the picture.

01

The line and the water

The painted mark is what the provider proved at startup. The water is what the caller demands with minimum_isolation. Water above the mark means the request is refused before any code runs. Change the controls and read the ticket.

Verified runsc paints the K mark. No floor is stated, so the water sits below every mark and the run is admitted.

Provider SANDBOX_PROVIDER

Runtime SANDBOX_DOCKER_RUNTIME

Egress guard E2B_GUARD_URL or SANDBOX_DOCKERCLOUD_GUARD_URL

Payload exactly one per Run

Grant grant_profile

Caller's floor minimum_isolation

dispatch ticketplimsolld · Run

    Nothing runs until somebody paints a line

    With SANDBOX_PROVIDER unset the daemon starts as the Disabled provider: every payload gets ErrDisabled, and no fallback exists. Not local Node, not the in-process engine. A provider is operator configuration, so a request can state a floor and be refused, but it can never promote the daemon to a stronger provider than the one configured.

    Two decisions, two people, two moments

    The tier is chosen by whoever configures the daemon, and demanded by whoever sends the request. The in-process tier exists for the edit-run-debug loop: no account, no key, no container daemon, no cost per run. The floor is what keeps that loop out of production: one field on the request, checked before dispatch, so a deployment that still carries wasm fails closed instead of quietly running hostile code in the daemon's own process.

    02

    Read the mark, not the name

    The same Docker provider paints two different marks depending on what it can prove. Every result reports the tier that actually ran, and the daemon can refuse to start below a tier with SANDBOX_MIN_ISOLATION. Weakest first.

    1. ·none
      Disabled safe refusal

      Nothing runs. A deployment may deliberately stay here.

    2. Pprocess
      WASM, QuickJS on wazero too weak for hostile code

      An engine boundary inside plimsolld. Memory is capped for real (wazero's memory pages, not a wrapper that reports a limit), but an engine escape lands in the daemon's own process. Fast, free, and not an operating-system wall.

    3. Ccontainer
      Docker on runc too weak alone

      A read-only root, sized noexec writable mounts, the network off, dropped capabilities, and optionally the shipped seccomp allowlist (SANDBOX_DOCKER_SECCOMP). An escape still reaches the shared host kernel.

    4. Kkernel
      Docker on verified runsc eligible

      The same container, but the runtime is gVisor: a user-space kernel takes the guest's syscalls before the host kernel ever sees them. The mark is painted only after Preflight verifies the runsc registration on the pinned daemon. That is configuration and behaviour evidence, not attestation of the running kernel.

    5. Vvm
      E2B or Docker Cloud Sandboxes, a microVM strongest

      A microVM is a small virtual machine with its own kernel, created for one run and destroyed after it. The boundary is hardware virtualisation, on somebody else's servers: E2B runs Firecracker microVMs, and Docker Cloud Sandboxes runs them on Docker-managed compute. The strongest wall, and the only tier that bills: both providers charge for the VMs they start.

    What a reported tier is, exactly. Configuration plus provider evidence plus the behavioural checks in 03. Never runtime attestation. A surface that advertises a tier has to carry that qualification, and this one does.

    03

    What a provider must prove before it serves

    Every real provider runs a startup smoke test that exercises behaviour, not just configuration, and none serves if it fails. The proofs are different because the rooms are different.

    Docker earns its mark in the mount table

    1. Pin one local daemon. One Unix endpoint, resolved once and reused; a remote daemon is refused because the per-run broker socket and the teardown would not hold.
    2. Verify the runtime. Inspect the daemon's registration, including the runsc executable path. Only a verified registration paints K; a failed refresh fails readiness closed.
    3. Inspect both images. Present and inspectable; an image that declares a VOLUME is rejected, because docker would auto-create an unbounded writable host volume for it. Every run then launches the content-addressed image ID that was inspected, so re-pointing a tag cannot smuggle a different image past the check.
    4. One throwaway container per image. From its own mount table it must show a read-only root and every writable mount as a tmpfs of the promised size with noexec and nosuid; then, by attempting a write at every mount point, that those are the only places a write lands.
    5. Reach a host socket. The first probe mounts a throwaway Unix socket the way a run mounts its broker socket and must connect to it. Under runsc that needs --host-uds=open; a runtime that cannot broker grants refuses to serve rather than fail every granted run.

    E2B earns its mark by creating a real VM

    1. Preflight is configuration only. It proves nothing about reachability, the key, or the template, which is why /readyz never creates a VM: a smoke test there would bill on every unauthenticated poll.
    2. One throwaway microVM at startup. Secured create with both access tokens, live resource verification against the configured maxima, multi-file staging into the project directory, and a probe run through the exact project-step path.
    3. Egress is checked live. The probe proves a no-grant VM cannot reach out. It establishes the deny-all floor; the guarded exception is proved separately by make e2b-guard-live, which fails rather than skips when unconfigured.
    4. Every VM is stamped. A per-instance metadata ID lets the daemon reap stamped, untracked VMs that leaked past a malformed create response or a failed teardown.

    The create response comes back without the secured envd token. The VM is addressable by its public URL, so a run could proceed. It does not: a public URL is not authority, the incomplete handle is rejected, and the VM is killed. The provider never downgrades its access contract to make a run succeed.

    Docker Cloud Sandboxes earns its mark the same way, and checks the seal on every run

    1. Preflight is configuration only, as for E2B, so /readyz never creates a sandbox.
    2. The token can do the job. The capability call must list the read, create, delete and network-policy-read permissions a run needs.
    3. One throwaway sandbox at startup. It must come up with its effective network policy at deny-all, accept a directory and file upload, and run the probe through the exact project-step path, proving the tools are present, the working directory is honoured, and egress is denied from inside the guest.
    4. The seal is read back on every run. The account's cloud network policy must default to deny-all (sbx --cloud policy init deny-all), because a create that carries its own policy fails. Each run reads the sandbox's effective policy back and refuses to run unless it is deny-all with nothing allowed.
    5. Every sandbox is named. A per-instance name prefix is recorded before the create is sent, so the daemon can delete untracked sandboxes it finds later.

    04

    A grant is a route, not the internet

    A run without a grant has no network. A run with one can reach exactly the routes an operator listed, through a broker that holds the credential outside the guest. Pick a design and read what the hostile code can observe.

    A profile lives in PLIMSOLL_GRANTS_FILE and holds the upstream origin, the allowed routes, an allowed_callers list of authenticated principals, the scopes, and how the credential is produced: one shared bearer from the environment, or a fresh short-lived JWT minted per run with the calling principal as its subject. The caller sends only the profile's name. A raw grant on the wire is refused, an empty route list reaches nothing, and declared scopes may not include code:run or *. The minter is called once per run.

    05

    Three channels, kept apart

    "Your code ran and failed", "we never ran your code" and "our plumbing broke" are three different facts, and each decides differently whether a retry is worth it.

    resultThe code ran. A non-zero exit is a normal answer with stdout, stderr and the tier it ran behind.
    typed refusalNothing ran. A named error before dispatch, with a Connect code a client can branch on.
    infrastructureSomething around the run broke. Never disguised as the guest's stderr.
    The guest calls process.exit(2) deliberately

    result Result.ExitCode is 2, no Go error. Output, duration, sandbox name and isolation all stay meaningful. Retrying changes nothing unless the code changes.

    The snippet is over 256 KiB shared validation

    typed refusal ErrInvalidRequest, InvalidArgument over RPC. Checked before any provider is touched. The same channel carries a malformed floor and an unknown profile name.

    The floor is above the mark section 01

    typed refusal ErrInsufficientIsolation, FailedPrecondition. No hostile code ran. The official client also re-checks the tier on the response; a mismatch there is ErrIsolationEvidenceMismatch, DataLoss, and it is never a safe automatic retry because execution may already have happened.

    Every admission slot is busy section 06

    typed refusal ErrAtCapacity, ResourceExhausted. Shed at once rather than queued, and a fair candidate for bounded backoff.

    A project's lint step fails stop on first failure

    result The step's exit code lives in Steps; the run's conclusion is ProjectResult.Outcome, one of completed, setup_failed, timed_out or protocol_error, with human context in Detail. A stable classification, not a string to parse.

    The container daemon disappears mid-run a dependency fails

    infrastructure An unmatched error, Internal over RPC. Output truncation, by contrast, is never an error: results carry StdoutTruncated and StderrTruncated flags and the retained bytes are never annotated in-band.

    06

    Admission: the smaller of two numbers

    Counting runs and reserving memory are different limits, and the daemon applies both. How many runs can be in flight is the run-count cap or the number of per-run envelopes that fit in the aggregate budget, whichever is smaller. Anything past that is shed on the spot, not queued. Twelve runs arrive at once; move the controls.

    The memory budget and the per-run envelope are set together or not at all, and a single run that needs more than the whole budget is a startup error, not a run that waits forever. E2B and Docker Cloud Sandboxes ignore the memory budget because their VMs live off this host; the count still applies. On top of the global gate, every caller has its own in-flight cap (SANDBOX_PER_KEY_CONCURRENT, half the global by default) and a token-bucket rate (SANDBOX_RATE_PER_MIN), so one busy tenant cannot take every berth.

    07

    Before you switch it on

    A provider is ready when every line below is true for the job in front of you, not when its name sounds strong enough. Tick what you have.
